title: 3-Read Friday #109: Gradual Release, Attainment Setting, and Atomisation
author: Craig Barton
summary: 3-Read Friday #109 opens with Mark Enser arguing that the 'I Do, We Do, You Do' gradual-release model only works when teachers genuinely release control, making expert thinking visible at each stage and accepting that productive struggle -- not extended scaffolding -- is the point where real learning begins. Becky Allen then argues that the evidence now closes the debate on setting by attainment in mathematics -- setting helps high attainers and harms no group -- while exposing a deeper, neglected problem: low-attaining pupils have heterogeneous needs that no grouping policy alone, only specialised diagnosis and intervention, can address. Kris Boulton closes with a concrete, example-heavy piece showing that Atomisation lets teachers identify and focus instruction on only the genuinely new atoms in a cognitive routine, wherever they sit in the chain, building deep conceptual mastery before students attempt the full process end to end. Barton frames Allen's piece as resolving the surface debate on setting while surfacing the harder question schools have been avoiding.
points: Enser's core claim about 'I Do, We Do, You Do': the model fails when teachers don't genuinely release control at the 'You Do' stage -- productive struggle, not prolonged scaffolding, is where the actual learning happens.

Allen's setting-in-maths verdict: the evidence closes the debate -- setting helps high attainers and harms no group -- but the real unresolved problem is the heterogeneous needs of low attainers, which grouping policy alone cannot fix.

Boulton's Atomisation walkthrough shows the payoff of the framework concretely: isolate only the genuinely new atoms in a cognitive routine, wherever they occur in the chain, rather than re-teaching the whole process every time.
Barton treats Allen's piece as effectively settling a long-running policy argument while reframing what schools should actually be worried about next.
quotes: Regular readers will know I love nothing more than a bit of I Do, We Do, You Do.
